The Bluespotted seabass Cephalopholis taeniops exhibits life-history traits typical of a moderately slow-growing epinephelid. Although empirical data specific to this species remain limited from the eastern Atlantic, comparative information from the closely related congener Cephalopholis cyanostigma provides useful insights. At a water temperature of 19.2 °C [T = 19.2 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) of mature females was approximately 3% [GSI = approximately 3%]. This relatively low value suggests a conservative reproductive investment per unit of body mass, a pattern often observed in serranids inhabiting structurally complex reef environments where spawning aggregations are temporally constrained. The same thermal regime influences early developmental rates; at 19.2 °C [T = 19.2 °C], the embryonic period lasts approximately 12 days [ab = approximately 12 days], after which the yolk-sac larva emerges. The duration of this egg stage is notably extended compared to tropical serranids, reflecting the moderating influence of the subtropical Canary Current waters where this species is frequently recorded. Hatchlings at emergence are minute, with the wet weight at birth calculated from the average egg diameter of 0.95 millimeters as 0.00045 grams [Wwb = 0.00045 grams].

The species follows a determinate growth trajectory that can be characterized by a length-weight relationship derived from field-collected specimens. The ultimate total length, representing the asymptotic maximum size attained by the largest individuals in the population, has been estimated at 70 centimeters [Li = 70 centimeters]. This places Cephalopholis taeniops among the medium-bodied members of its genus, comparable in terminal size to the Rock hind Epinephelus adscensionis within the same geographic range. Corresponding to this asymptotic length, the ultimate wet weight calculated from the empirical length-weight scaling relationship is approximately 5246 grams [Wwi = approximately 5246 grams]. Such a body size implies a relatively high trophic position, as large-bodied serranids are typically piscivorous ambush predators that require substantial home ranges on rocky and coralline substrates. The growth pattern suggests that individuals allocate considerable resources to somatic tissue accumulation before reaching a plateau, a strategy that delays the onset of reproductive activity. Field observations indicate that the total length at which 50 percent of the population attains sexual maturity is 18 centimeters [Lp = 18 centimeters], a value that corresponds to an estimated wet weight at puberty of 78 grams [Wwp = 78 grams].

This significant size discrepancy between puberty and asymptotic length underscores a life-history strategy in which sexual maturation occurs relatively early in the somatic growth trajectory, a pattern common among serranids that exhibit protogynous sex change. At a total length of 18 centimeters [Lp = 18 centimeters], individuals are functionally mature females capable of contributing to the local spawning stock, yet they have achieved only a fraction of their ultimate somatic potential. The derived wet weight at puberty of 78 grams [Wwp = 78 grams] is less than 1.5 percent of the ultimate wet weight, indicating that early reproductive investment is initiated while individuals are still in a phase of rapid mass gain. This early onset of maturation may be an adaptive response to moderate levels of fishing pressure, which selectively removes larger, older individuals from the population. In comparison to other epinephelids, such as the Nassau grouper Epinephelus striatus, which matures at a larger relative size, Cephalopholis taeniops appears to prioritize an earlier age at first reproduction, potentially enhancing population resilience under exploitation. The growth coefficient embedded in the length-weight equation used to derive the mass values is consistent with isometric or slightly positive allometric scaling.

Life-history theory predicts that early maturation at a small body size is often coupled with a relatively short lifespan, yet available data for Cephalopholis taeniops indicate a substantial maximum longevity. Based on mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age validation conducted at a water temperature of 19.2 °C [T = 19.2 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan for this species is 20 years [am = 20 years]. This extended lifespan, equivalent to approximately 7300 days, is remarkable for a serranid that initiates reproduction at a modest 18 centimeters in total length. The longevity suggests that post-reproductive survival is high, and that individuals may continue to grow and reproduce across multiple decades, albeit at a declining rate as they approach their asymptotic length of 70 centimeters [Li = 70 centimeters]. Such a pattern is consistent with the bet-hedging reproductive strategy observed in long-lived marine fishes, where iteroparous spawning over many seasons buffers against interannual recruitment failures. The sustained presence of older individuals in the population also contributes to the reproductive output, as larger females produce disproportionately more and larger eggs. In the context of the subtropical upwelling ecosystem off the coast of West Africa, this longevity may buffer the species against environmental stochasticity in food availability.

The egg diameter of 0.95 millimeters, from which the wet weight at birth of 0.00045 grams [Wwb = 0.00045 grams] was derived, is comparatively large for a serranid, indicating a pelagic larval stage that benefits from substantial maternal provisioning. The ultimate wet weight of 5246 grams [Wwi = 5246 grams] is achieved only late in life, reinforcing the interpretation that the species invests heavily in somatic capital across its extended 20-year lifespan (20 years) [am = 20 years] at a temperature of 19.2 °C [T = 19.2 °C]. Population modeling that incorporates these life-history parameters suggests that the species has a low intrinsic rate of increase, making it vulnerable to overfishing if mature individuals are removed before they have had the opportunity to reproduce across multiple spawning seasons. Conservation strategies should therefore focus on maintaining the spawning stock biomass of individuals exceeding the 18-centimeter total length at puberty threshold (18 centimeters) [Lp = 18 centimeters].
